md: This argument explains the *direction* of a single step, with moving averages switched off. It says nothing about momentum: Bernstein and Newhouse treat the averages as smoothing against mini-batch noise, and call their exact role an open question. Muon adds momentum for empirical reasons.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Choosing an optimizer: how much faster is it really?
md: An optimizer claim is only as good as its baseline. Ask: was the baseline tuned as hard, at more than one scale and data ratio, compared at the end of training, and in which unit (steps, tokens, FLOPs or hours)? Independent tests put matrix optimizers ahead of AdamW, by less than first reported.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Deriving the rules from one condition, and muP by hand
md: One rule generates muP: every weight and every update should have spectral norm about the square root of fan_out over fan_in. For Adam that means learning rate 1/fan_in for every layer; for SGD, fan_out/fan_in.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: From a racy flag to a correct spin lock
md: Atomic does not mean cheap. An atomic write to a line that other cores are reading forces cache-line transfers, and in Bos's measurement it made another core's plain loads about 10 times slower on an older x86-64 machine.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Why a database keeps old copies of rows
md: MVCC trades space for concurrency: every update leaves an old version behind so that readers already in flight can keep a consistent view without blocking writers.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Paying for versions: VACUUM, HOT updates and XID wraparound
md: MVCC moves the cost of concurrency into the storage engine: dead versions to clean, index entries to maintain, and XIDs to freeze. Long-lived snapshots make all three worse.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Three branches: compress, select, and slide
md: The gates are independent sigmoids, not a softmax. They do not have to sum to 1, so the model can turn several branches up or down at once. Also note what NSA does *not* do: it keeps the full KV cache (and three branches with independent keys and values), so it cuts the bytes *read* per step, not the bytes *stored*.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: Searching millions of hashes: BK-trees and multi-index hashing
md: MIH is fast only when substring buckets stay small. Norouzi et al. analyze uniformly distributed codes and find a substring length of about log2 of the database size works well. Highly skewed hashes (many near-blank images with the same hash) create giant buckets. PDQ's quality score, a 0 to 100 measure of how much detail an image has (next lesson), flags such featureless images so they can be filtered out.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: ARP spoofing up close, and how switches stop it
md: Static ARP entries on every laptop are not a practical fix: they break when hardware changes and do not scale. Put the check in the switch (DHCP snooping plus DAI), where one configuration covers every port, and encrypt traffic so a successful poisoner learns little.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Firewalls: stateless, stateful and application-aware
md: A firewall that allows port 443 allows every attack that arrives over port 443. Firewalls decide who may talk to whom on which port; whether the conversation itself is malicious is the job of the application, TLS, and IDS or application-layer inspection.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Suricata in depth: how rules match, EVE output and tuning
md: Every Suricata alert should send you to the flow behind it: pull the EVE records with the same flow_id (or the Zeek logs with the same Community ID) and decide from the full conversation, not from the alert message alone.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Network forensics for incident response: a worked IcedID investigation
md: Network forensics is pivoting with discipline: logs to scope, packets to prove, one UTC timeline, every step recorded. The attacker controls the infected host; they rarely control your sensor.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: UDP and ICMP: no handshake, and messages about the network
md: "Block all ICMP" is a common overreaction. It hides hosts from ping sweeps, but it also breaks useful signals such as fragmentation needed (type 3, code 4), which hosts rely on to size their packets. Filter selectively: allow the error messages your network needs, rate-limit echo, and log the rest.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Memory policies: local, bind, preferred and interleave
md: Setting a policy does not move pages that already exist. `mbind(2)` affects only new allocations unless you pass the flag `MPOL_MF_MOVE` (or `MPOL_MF_MOVE_ALL`, which also moves pages that other processes share, and so needs CAP_SYS_NICE, a Linux capability: one of the slices of root privilege a process can hold). Install the policy before the first touch, or ask for migration explicitly.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Parallel flash and the NVMe queue interface
md: NVMe queue depth does not make flash faster; it lets the controller keep many dies busy. One synchronous 4 KB read at a time pays the full read latency per request no matter how many queues the drive has. Use async I/O (io_uring, the Linux asynchronous I/O interface built on shared submission and completion rings; SPDK, or many threads) to keep enough requests in flight.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Counting objects: by detection, by density, by tracking
md: A density map gives a number, not a list of objects. You cannot crop, identify or follow an individual from it, and the count is real-valued. Use it when objects are too dense to box, not as a default.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: What metrics, traces and logs can each answer
md: A common misconception: "we log everything, so we are observable". Logs scale with traffic times fields per event, metrics scale with the number of distinct label combinations, and traces scale with the sampling rate. Choosing where each fact lives is the design work.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Why OCR is a pipeline: find the text, then read it
md: A common bug: cropping a single field, such as a price, and running Tesseract with the default `--psm 3`. Automatic page segmentation expects a page and can find no lines at all in a tight crop. Use `--psm 7` (one line) or `--psm 8` (one word), and leave a small white border around the text.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Judging answers on documents with ANLS
md: ANLS cannot tell a harmless typo from a costly one: `42.50` predicted as `42.5` scores 0.8, the same as many genuine digit errors of similar size. For money and IDs, add field-level exact match after normalization.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: chroot is not a boundary, and Leaky Vessels shows why
md: chroot changes how paths are looked up, nothing more. Open file descriptors, the working directory and root's privileges all ignore it. Real filesystem isolation needs a mount namespace, no privilege to undo it, and no handles that point outside.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Requirements and collection plans: decide before you search
md: No requirement, no collection. A plan that names sources, legal basis and retention keeps an investigation focused, defensible and small.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Geolocation: finding where a picture was taken
md: Geolocate places and events, not private people. Working out where a private individual lives or goes from their photos is stalking, whatever the technique is called. Practise on public landmarks, games built for it, or published case studies.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Putting it together: an ethical OSINT review, and where to practise
md: Never practise on real private people, including friends who "don't mind". Use public landmarks, fictional scenarios, practice platforms, and your own organisation with written permission.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: What CI does when you open a pull request
md: A green local run does not prove CI will pass. CI tests your change merged into the latest base branch, on a clean machine, often across several OS and Python versions. Read the workflow file to see what will actually run.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: What a reviewer is deciding: the code-health standard
md: Approve when the change makes the codebase better than it was, not when it matches what you would have written. There is no perfect code, only better code. The goal is continuous improvement.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Where a project's rules live and how GitHub finds them
md: A repository with no `CONTRIBUTING.md` in its file list may still have one. It can be in `.github/` or `docs/`, or inherited from the organization's `.github` repository, which never shows up in the repository's own files or clone. Use the link GitHub shows on the new issue or PR page.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Fork, clone and two remotes: origin and upstream
md: Fetch from `upstream`, push to `origin`. Remote-tracking branches like `upstream/main` are snapshots from your last fetch, not live views.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Sign-off, the DCO, and how your commits land upstream
md: `-s` adds a Signed-off-by trailer whose meaning the project defines (often the DCO). Read CONTRIBUTING to learn whether the project wants sign-offs, fixups squashed, and which merge method it uses.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: The DCO: certifying every commit with Signed-off-by
md: A sign-off you add without reading the DCO is still a legal statement about provenance. Copying code you cannot trace (a gist without a license, generated output in a project that bans it) and signing off is exactly what the DCO exists to prevent.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Regression checks: perf bots and noise thresholds from history
md: Regression checks only work if noise is known. A bot learns each benchmark's normal spread from history and flags changes beyond it; you do the same by hand with repeated, interleaved runs and a test.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Shrinking a failing program by hand
md: "Same problem" means the *same* failure, not just any failure. If removing a line turns a `StatisticsError` into a `NameError`, you did not shrink the bug; you created a new one. Compare the exception type and message every time, not just whether something crashed.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: Why a reviewer sends a big pull request back
md: Misconception: "small" means "tiny". Google's guide also says a change can be too small to understand: if you add a new API, include a use of it in the same change so reviewers can judge it.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Block tables: virtual memory for the KV cache
md: The block table is the whole trick: contiguous logical blocks, scattered physical blocks, allocation on demand. Waste is capped at one partly filled block per sequence.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Authorisation: scope, rules of engagement and permission
md: If something is not written in the scope, it is out of scope. When a new system appears mid-test (a subdomain, an extra address range), stop and get written approval to add it. PTES names scope creep as a common failure, especially during retesting.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Reporting: from finding to fix, and the retest
md: A finding is done when the client can understand it, verify it safely, fix the cause as well as the symptom, and see it marked closed after a retest.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: A profiling workflow, its costs and its blind spots
md: The workflow: record with a modest rate and working stacks, fold, filter, draw, read top edges, fix the widest plateau that you can change, then measure again.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: The persuasion levers every lure pulls
md: Misconception: "spotting bad grammar catches phishing". Spelling mistakes were never the core of a lure, and well-written messages are now easy to produce: the FBI's 2025 IC3 report notes businesses reported over USD 30 million in losses to BEC scams involving AI. Train on the levers and the process rules, not on typos.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Layered defences and the analyst workflow for a reported phish
md: The NCSC also warns that punishing people for clicking simulated phish erodes trust and stops them reporting real mistakes; it starts to resemble entrapment. Teach the levers and process rules (lesson 2), make reporting effortless, and celebrate reports.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Rust layout: default repr, repr(C), and niches
md: C keeps your field order and you are responsible for packing it well. Rust's default repr may reorder fields and use niches to save space, but promises no exact layout. Use `#[repr(C)]` whenever bytes cross a boundary your compiler does not control.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Five families, one competition and two spectacular breaks
md: What defenders take from 2022: young algorithms can fail completely, and to classical math. Hence three habits used throughout this course: **hybrids** during the transition (security holds if either component does), **diversity** (HQC as a backup on different math; SLH-DSA relying only on hashes) and **crypto agility**, so that replacing an algorithm is a configuration change rather than a rewrite.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Post-filtering: why top-k comes back short
md: Database textbooks sometimes say a filter is *highly selective* when it keeps very few rows, the opposite direction to the ratio. When reading docs, check whether they mean the ratio $s$ or the strictness. Here, small $s$ always means few matches.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Little's law: how many misses must be in flight
md: **Prefetching is a way to raise concurrency.** A prefetch is a miss started early, before the program's own load. Anything that lets more independent misses overlap (prefetchers, unrolled loops, several independent lists walked at once, more threads) moves you up the curve.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Sparse data: how a few ratings re-identified Netflix users
md: In sparse, high-dimensional data, every person is an outlier. A handful of rare facts, even noisy ones, is enough to find a record, and then the whole record is exposed.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: The Laplace mechanism: calibrating noise, worked
md: Never let users re-run a noisy query for free. Repeated noisy answers can be averaged; composition counts every one. Cache answers or charge each run to the budget.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Privacy threat modelling with LINDDUN
md: Do not treat LINDDUN as a compliance checklist. Its value is the same as STRIDE's: asking each element and flow "how could this hurt the people in the data?" before the design is fixed.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a privacy review, and where to practise
md: A privacy review asks, in order: what data actions happen, how they could hurt people (LINDDUN), whether the processing is necessary (DPIA), what must leave the system and the matching technique (DP, PSI, secure aggregation, or not releasing), how the design minimises, and how rights reach every copy.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Grading the answer versus grading every step
md: A correct final answer does not mean correct reasoning. On GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021: about 8,500 grade-school math word problems), Uesato et al. found that RL directly against final-answer correctness left a best **trace error** (any human-judged mistake in the reasoning, among answer-correct solutions) of 12.4%, versus 3.8% for their best process-based method.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Failure modes, evaluation, and why some labs skip PRMs
md: Do not judge a PRM only by best-of-N accuracy. That metric checks final answers, rewards PRMs that act like outcome models, and depends on which generator produced the samples. Check step-level error location (for example ProcessBench) on the distribution you will actually run it on.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Who runs next: run queues, CFS, EEVDF and nice
md: Linux runs, on each CPU, a task that has not had more than its weighted fair share: CFS picks the smallest vruntime; EEVDF picks, among eligible tasks (lag of zero or more), the earliest virtual deadline. Nice values set weights 1.25x apart; slices end on ticks and wakeups, and those are your involuntary switches.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Why hand-tuned prompts are brittle
md: Misconception: "a prompt that works is a good prompt". A hand-tuned prompt is fitted to one model, one task and the handful of examples you looked at. Change the model, the data or even the separator characters and the ranking of prompts can change.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: Sequence design, then the self-consistency check
md: Self-consistency grades a generator with a predictor that was trained on natural proteins, and both can be wrong in the same direction. A design that AF2 loves is not proven to fold: it has passed one cheap filter. Everything after this point costs money and weeks.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Reading CSV exports and JSON records without breaking them
md: Never split CSV or JSON by hand. `csv.DictReader` and `json.loads` implement the quoting and escaping rules you would otherwise get wrong, and wrong parsing in security tooling means missed indicators.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Vocabulary mismatch: why BM25 misses relevant documents
md: Better scoring cannot fix a zero-overlap miss. Query expansion changes **which documents can match at all** by adding terms to the query (or, in document expansion, to the documents). That is a recall tool first, and every added term is also a new way to match the wrong document.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Paying for it: latency, cost and when not to rewrite
md: Misconception: rewriting is free accuracy. Besides latency and cost, a rewriter can **drift** from the user's intent (RAG-Fusion's evaluation saw off-topic answers from unrelated generated queries) and it is a new failure point (timeouts, malformed output). Keep the original query as a fallback or as one of the queries, and log every rewrite next to the original so you can audit drift.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Business logic flaws: when correct code does the wrong thing
md: Misconception: "we validate all input, so we are safe". Format checks (is it an integer, is it a known product) do not test meaning (is this quantity possible, is this step allowed now, has this coupon been used). Logic flaws live in the meaning.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Case: Starbucks gift cards and two browser sessions (2015)
md: Protect the resource being spent, not the path to it. A one-time flag in the session, a disabled button or a cleared form all guard one route to the balance; a lock or atomic update on the balance itself guards every route.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Testing logic: invariants, abuse cases and concurrency tests
md: Write the invariant first, then a test that tries to break it in every way this course showed: odd values, odd order, and many at once. A test suite with no parallel test cannot fail on a race.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Consensus in production: reads, membership, timeouts
md: Consensus is safe without any timing assumptions; timing only buys availability. Every production feature here (reads, reconfiguration, Pre-Vote) is checked against the same question: can two majorities that do not overlap make conflicting decisions?

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Document, query and interaction signals: freshness, popularity, clicks
md: Shape raw signals before the model sees them: turn age into a decaying freshness, counts into logs or rates, and remember that query-only features can only matter through interactions.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Is the difference real? Paired tests, effect sizes, many systems
md: Compare systems on per-query differences, with a paired t-test or randomization test, and report the mean difference with a confidence interval and effect size. With many systems, control the familywise error instead of running dozens of independent tests.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Hardening that actually blocks the path
md: Joining hypervisors, backup servers and RMM consoles to the production domain feels tidy, but it gives whoever owns AD the keys to everything at once. Separate authentication for these systems is the single design choice that most often decides whether a domain compromise becomes a business-ending outage.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: InfiniBand, RoCEv2 and iWARP: what carries the packets
md: RoCEv2 gets RDMA onto ordinary routed Ethernet only by making that Ethernet (nearly) lossless with PFC, then taming PFC's side effects with end-to-end congestion control such as DCQCN. Loss is still possible from corruption or misconfiguration, and go-back-N recovery makes it expensive.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Showing other players: interpolation and lag compensation
md: The local player lives in the **present** (prediction); everyone else is shown in the **past** (interpolation); the server reconciles the two when it matters (lag compensation).

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Cold start: content for new items, bandits for new users
md: Cold start is a data problem, so the fixes are other data: content features for new items, context and popularity for new users, then controlled exploration to collect the interactions CF needs.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: When each join wins: row counts, probes and memory
md: `work_mem` is a limit per sort or hash operation, not per query. A plan with three hash joins and a sort can use several multiples of it, and many sessions can do so at once. Raising it globally to fix one query can exhaust memory.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Failures: sloppy quorums, hinted handoff and repair
md: A write that *fails* (fewer than W acks before the timeout) is not rolled back. It may sit on a minority of replicas and later spread through repair or hints. The Cassandra docs warn that without blocking read repair such a write "may be visible in one read, and then disappear in a subsequent read". "Failed" means "outcome unknown", not "did not happen".

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: Fixing the reward, not just the leash: ensembles, WARM, ODIN, PAR
md: Every reward-side fix encodes an assumption about *where* the reward is wrong: in members' disagreement, in label noise, in a named feature, or in extreme values. Hacks that live outside that assumption pass straight through, so these methods complement an outside check; they do not replace it.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Assessing risk in practice: from asset list to risk register
md: Multiplying ordinal numbers (ranks, like 1 to 5) treats the gap between 4 and 5 as equal to the gap between 1 and 2, which is rarely true of real losses. Grids are fine for sorting a long list quickly and for talking to non-specialists. They are not fine for deciding whether a USD 300,000 control is worth buying. For that, estimate in money.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: NIST CSF 2.0: six functions, profiles and tiers
md: Misconception: "we implemented the CSF". The CSF lists outcomes, not controls; you cannot install it. Saying you *use* it means you have profiles, owners for the gaps and a review cycle. A slide with the six function names is not alignment.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Compliance as code: policy checks in CI and automatic evidence
md: A control that runs as code on every change is both stronger security and better evidence: the CI logs show it ran on every pull request all year, and the evidence store shows the state on any date an auditor picks. Failing the build is the cheapest moment to fix a compliance gap.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Cyber insurance: what it pays, what it asks, what it excludes
md: Cyber insurance transfers part of the financial tail: forensics, restoration, business interruption, liability. It is priced and conditioned on your controls; misstatements can void claims. Model deductible and limit against your loss distribution, read the exclusions (fraud, war and state-backed attacks), and keep the application as true as your SOC 2.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Weight sync: resharding and moving the bytes every step
md: Sync cost = bytes / bandwidth + resharding. The bytes are fixed by model size and precision; good systems avoid gathering the full model anywhere, send each rank only its shard, and keep the transfer off the critical path.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: Walking the dependency graph to the anomalous frontier
md: Correlation is not causation, and the SRE troubleshooting chapter names the two ways this bites. First, correlated events often share a cause: packet loss in a cluster and failed disks in the same cluster correlate because a power event hit both, not because either caused the other. Second, as you monitor more metrics it becomes inevitable that some will correlate well with your symptom purely by coincidence.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Ties, missing documents and the window size
md: Pagination: in Elasticsearch, if `from + size` (results skipped plus the page length) exceeds `rank_window_size` you get 0 results, and pages are only consistent while `rank_window_size` stays fixed. Changing W re-ranks everything, as the animation shows, so never vary it between page requests.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Locks and refcounts as types: Guard, Opaque and Arc
md: The pattern is always the same: an `unsafe` C protocol (lock and unlock, get and put, register and unregister) becomes a value whose constructor does the first half and whose `Drop` does the second. The type system then tracks the protocol for every caller.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Dispatch queues: how tasks travel from BPF to a CPU
md: A CPU only ever runs tasks from its own local DSQ. Everything else (global DSQ, custom DSQs, BPF maps) is staging. The pick order is local, then global, then `ops.dispatch()`.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Placement and preemption: idle CPUs, kicks, LOCAL_ON and locality
md: Placement is decided when a task lands in a local DSQ. `select_cpu` and the idle cpumask choose where, `LOCAL_ON` puts it there from any CPU, and kicks (`IDLE`, `PREEMPT`) decide when that CPU looks.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Secrets: what they are, how long they live, why they sprawl
md: A secret's danger is what it opens, times how long it works, times how many places it lives. Every technique in this course shrinks one of those three: least privilege shrinks the first, rotation and dynamic secrets the second, vaults and scanning the third.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: The end state: workload identity instead of stored secrets
md: The best secret is one that does not exist at rest. Where one must exist, make it short-lived, unique to one consumer, held in one audited place and rotated automatically with overlap.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: JavaScript: prototype pollution and code built from strings
md: Any code that writes `obj[key] = value` with a key from input, or walks nested input recursively, must refuse `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype`, or use objects with no prototype. Any string that reaches eval, Function or a string timer is code injection.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Compiler warnings and hardening flags a C reviewer should demand
md: Warnings find bugs; hardening flags limit the damage of the bugs you missed. Review build files like code: a change that removes either, or adds -Wno-format-security or -fno-stack-protector, needs the same scrutiny as a change to authentication.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: IPsec building blocks: SAs, SPIs, ESP, AH and two modes
md: A common misconception: tunnel mode is not more encrypted than transport mode. Both use the same ESP encryption. Tunnel mode additionally hides the inner addresses and lets a gateway protect traffic for a whole network; transport mode is for two hosts protecting their own traffic.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Encrypting email itself: S/MIME, OpenPGP and EFAIL (2018)
md: EFAIL's root cause was releasing unauthenticated plaintext into an active renderer (HTML that fetches URLs). Authenticated encryption plus a strict rule (verify first, show nothing on failure) removes the gadget attack; disabling remote content in the client removes the easiest exfiltration channel.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Inside BeyondCorp: inventory, trust tiers and the access proxy
md: In an access-proxy design the device inventory and the identity system are part of the trusted computing base. If the inventory says a stolen laptop is healthy, every check downstream agrees.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: From a script to a pipeline: the parts of a security automation
md: A security automation is a small distributed system that holds powerful credentials and processes data attackers can influence. Design for duplicates, partial failure and hostile input from the first version.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Measuring AI triage: golden sets, precision, recall and attack success
md: Golden-set labels must come from completed investigations. If you label with first-look verdicts, you measure how well the model copies hurried humans, including their misses.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Who attacks and why: criminals, states, insiders, activists
md: Ask "who would want this asset, and what would they do with it?" Criminals want quick money and reuse easy entry points such as stolen passwords. States want long, quiet access. Insiders already have access. The defence emphasis differs for each, but removing unused access helps against all of them.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: The attack lifecycle: kill chain and MITRE ATT&CK
md: Kill chain: seven phases, and breaking any link stops the intrusion. ATT&CK: tactics (why) and techniques (how) with IDs, the shared language of detection rules and threat reports.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Risk memos and exceptions: making someone own the decision
md: An exception is a decision with a name, a reason, compensating controls and an end date. Without all four it is just an unfixed vulnerability that someone has stopped looking at.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Inside the search tree: selection, expansion, evaluation and backup
md: Backup is where look-ahead becomes knowledge: exact outcomes and value estimates deep in the tree are averaged into the root's $Q$ values, with the sign flipped at every ply so each player maximizes their own result. The visit counts that result are the improved policy the network imitates.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Inventing the tasks: Absolute Zero and what bounds every loop
md: For any self-improvement claim, ask two questions: what outside the current model decides that a sample is good, and how often is it wrong? The loop can only improve as far as that signal is informative.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: The server as a confused deputy
md: The server is trusted by its network, its cloud account and its own disk. Any feature that lets input choose *what the server touches* (a host, a path, a class, a lookup) lends that trust to the attacker. Defence means taking the choice away, or shrinking what the server can touch.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Path traversal and safe path joins
md: Common broken fixes: deleting `../` from the input once (nested sequences reassemble after the deletion), checking before URL-decoding (encoded dots slip through), checking the string starts with the base (`/srv/app/files-old` passes), and forgetting that on Windows the backslash `..\` works too. Normalise first, then compare whole path components.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Turning a road map into a weighted directed graph
md: A road network is a large, sparse, directed graph with **nonnegative** weights. Every fast routing algorithm in this course depends on the weights never being negative.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: The DFT: one dot product per complex sinusoid
md: The DFT is a matrix-vector product: $N$ dot products of the signal with orthogonal complex sinusoids. Each $X[k]$ says how much of frequency $k$ is present (magnitude) and where it starts (phase), and the inverse DFT rebuilds $x$ exactly.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Why speedups fall short: latency chains and the memory wall
md: Misconception: "my SIMD loop is slow, so I need wider vectors." If it streams from DRAM with little math per byte, it is memory-bound and AVX-512 will not help. Measure bytes per second against your machine's bandwidth first.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: The buddy allocator: split in halves, merge with one XOR
md: Buddy trades internal fragmentation (power-of-two rounding, up to about 50 percent) for fast, simple coalescing: the buddy is one XOR away. It suits page-granular, physically contiguous memory, which is why Linux uses it for its page allocator and builds smaller allocators on top.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Generating data: the rollout loop and your own functions
md: Put per-sample agent logic in a custom generate function and scoring in a custom reward function. You keep slime's batching, dynamic sampling, abort and partial-rollout machinery for free, and your code works unchanged under fully async rollout.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: When the attacker calls the help desk: MFA resets and new devices
md: The help desk is part of your attack surface and part of your sensor network. Alert on MFA resets and new device enrollments for privileged users, correlate them with what happens next, and verify with the real person through a channel the caller cannot control. Okta also recommends stronger help desk identity checks, such as visual verification.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Security is a secondary task: why people work around it
md: Misconception: "people ignore security because they do not care". Adams and Sasse found people inventing their own schemes to comply, and Herley shows that ignoring costly advice is often the rational choice. When most people bypass a control, treat it as a design defect in the control.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Physical security in layers: zones, CPTED and access rules
md: Misconception: "physical security is the facilities team's job". Many intrusion paths end at a network port or an unlocked laptop. Security engineers should own the requirements (which zones protect which systems, what gets logged, how alerts reach the SOC) together with facilities.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Enforcing sparsity: L1, TopK and JumpReLU
md: L1 penalises size, so it shrinks every active latent. TopK (fixed k), Gated (separate gate) and JumpReLU (learned per-latent thresholds with an L0 penalty) all separate deciding which latents fire from estimating how big they are.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Where SAEs fall short: absorption, missing features and weak baselines
md: Sparsity rewards absorbing a parent feature into its children, so SAE latents can have silent holes. Matryoshka and BatchTopK reduce the damage, but SAEs are not canonical units, and on labelled tasks simple baselines such as difference-in-means and linear probes usually match or beat them.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Ordinary kriging: solving for the best weights
md: Kriging weights come from solving a linear system, not from a fixed formula. That lets them account for redundancy between sensors (declustering) and for sensors hidden behind others (screening), and it yields an error variance for every estimate.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Speculative sampling: guesses that keep the target's distribution
md: Accept with $\min(1, p/q)$, on rejection sample from $\text{norm}(\max(0, p - q))$, where norm rescales to sum to 1. Accepted mass is $\min(p, q)$ and residual mass is $p - \min(p, q)$; they add up to $p$ for any draft.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Word error rate: alignments, normalization and fair comparisons
md: Only compare WER numbers computed with the same normalizer on the same references. Switching normalizers, or counting *you're* versus *you are* as an error, can move WER more than a model upgrade. For languages written without spaces, character error rate (CER) is used instead.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The heap: free lists, chunk headers and where malloc gets memory
md: Stack: LIFO, bounded, freed by returning, one instruction. Heap: any order, any size, any lifetime, paid for with headers, rounding, free-list searches and fragmentation.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Page faults: lazy allocation, copy-on-write and overcommit
md: Most page faults are normal: they are how Linux allocates memory on first touch and copies pages only on write. Count them with getrusage or `perf stat -e page-faults,major-faults`; worry about major faults and fault storms, not their existence.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: When steering fails: unreliable inputs and the prompting baseline
md: Steering is a research and monitoring tool before it is a product control. Use it when you need to know *which* internal direction drives a behavior, to detect a concept, or to add to a prompt (CAA's vectors still moved behavior on top of system prompts). Always report per-input effects, a random vector of equal norm and a prompting baseline; without them a mean effect proves little.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Downsampling, retention and exactly-once vs at-least-once
md: End-to-end exactly-once needs three parts: a replayable source (Kafka offsets), consistent state (checkpoints), and an output that is transactional or idempotent (upsert by a deterministic key such as sensor and window). Duplicates created upstream, such as MQTT QoS 1 retries, must be removed by id.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Multi-head attention by hand: two heads, two patterns
md: Multi-head attention = several narrow attention functions in parallel, each free to learn a different pattern, at roughly the cost of one wide head.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Why raw TF-IDF ranks a keyword-stuffed page first
md: BM25 is still a sum over query terms of (IDF) x (a term-frequency factor). What changes is the term-frequency factor: it is bounded and length-aware instead of a raw count.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Causal self-attention: each position may only look backward
md: The causal mask is the only thing that makes this a *decoder*. Remove it and you have an encoder block; keep it and every position's prediction depends only on its prefix, so one pass trains all $T$ positions honestly.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: A derivative is the slope you see when you zoom in
md: The derivative is not the change in $f$ over a big step. It is a rate at one point. For $x^2$ at 3, a step of $+2$ actually raises $f$ by 16, not $6 \times 2 = 12$, because the slope itself changes along the way. This is exactly why **gradient descent**, the training method that repeatedly moves every parameter a small step downhill (lesson 6), takes small steps.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: The multivariable chain rule: summing over every path
md: Multiply local derivatives along each path, then add over all paths from the input to the output. Fan-out in the forward pass becomes a sum in the backward pass.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Files, paths and permissions: finding your way around
md: A mode is nine bits in three groups of rwx (owner, group, others), written as three octal digits with r = 4, w = 2, x = 1. On a file, x means run it; on a directory, x means enter it. Exactly one group applies to you.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Searching and transforming text: grep, regex, find, sed and awk
md: `sed -i` edits a file in place, and it differs between systems. GNU sed (Linux) takes an optional backup suffix glued to the flag, so `sed -i 's/a/b/' f` works. BSD sed (macOS) requires the suffix argument, so the same command takes the script as the suffix and fails. `sed -i.bak 's/a/b/' f` works on both and keeps the original as `f.bak`.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Your environment and remote machines: dotfiles, ssh and tmux
md: Login shells read ~/.bash_profile, other interactive shells ~/.bashrc, scripts neither. ssh logs you in with a key pair whose private half never leaves your machine, and tmux keeps remote work alive when the connection drops.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Beyond words: autoencoders and the InfoNCE loss
md: Embeddings come from an objective, not from the lookup table. Pick the objective so that items you want close (words in the same contexts, two views of one image, a user and the items they clicked) are pushed together and everything else is pushed apart.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: The KV cache: why memory grows with every token
md: KV cache size = 2 x layers x KV heads x head dim x bytes, per token, per sequence. It grows linearly with context and with batch size, and it is usually what limits how many users one GPU can serve.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: The CPU loop: fetch, decode, execute, repeat
md: Simplified: real CPUs pipeline and overlap many instructions, and even execute them out of order (lesson 7). But they are built so that the visible result is exactly as if each instruction ran one at a time in program order, which is why this model is the right one to reason with.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Why real CPUs beat the simple loop: pipelines and prediction
md: Misconception: "fewer instructions always means faster code." The two versions of the threshold loop do about the same work per element, yet one ran several times slower on random data. Predictability of branches, like the memory access pattern in lesson 6, can matter more than the instruction count.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Supervised fine-tuning: same loss, curated data, masked prompt
md: SFT = pretraining loss + chat template + loss only on response tokens (including the end-of-turn token) + a small, high-quality dataset.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: From grep to the inverted index
md: An inverted index alone does not rank anything. Boolean retrieval returns an unordered set: a document either matches or it does not. Ranking needs term weights, which lessons 4 and 5 add on top of the same postings.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Inverted indexes in real engines: compression, updates, Lucene
md: TF-IDF still has two flaws that cosine only partly fixes: tf keeps growing with every repetition (keyword stuffing pays), and length normalization is crude. BM25, the next course, keeps the same inverted index and replaces the weighting with a saturating tf and a tunable length normalization.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Addresses and pointers: what int *p actually stores
md: A pointer is a variable whose value is an address. `&` takes an address, `*` follows one, and the pointer's type decides how many bytes are read or written at that address.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Structs and linked data: ->, typedef and a linked list
md: A struct is a named group of members; `.` selects a member and `->` selects one through a pointer. A linked list is nodes on the heap connected by pointers, and changing a list means rewriting the right link, which is why functions that change it take `node **`.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Debugging C: gdb and Valgrind on a real crash
md: Build with `-g -O0` when debugging. Read a backtrace from frame #0 down to your own code, then use breakpoints, next, step, finish and print to see why the state went wrong. Use watchpoints for 'who changed this', and Valgrind when you cannot rebuild.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Ownership in methods and loops: self, &self, &mut self and for
md: A method signature is an ownership contract: `&self` reads, `&mut self` modifies, `self` consumes. A `for` loop over `v` consumes it; over `&v` or `&mut v` it borrows.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Closures and threads: moving ownership to another thread
md: Adding `move` fixes E0373 by handing the value over, not by sharing it: the spawning function loses access. If both sides need the data, clone it before the spawn, or share it with `Arc`.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Matrix multiplication: composing maps and checking shapes
md: $(m \times n)(n \times p) = (m \times p)$. Each entry is a row-column dot product, the product means apply the right matrix first, and order matters.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Where it shows up: linear layers, batches and attention scores
md: Shape errors are the most common bug in ML code. Before running a line like `X @ W.T + b`, write the shapes next to it, `(B,n) @ (n,m) + (m,)`, and check that inner sizes match and the bias length equals the output size.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Classification end to end: logistic regression, boundaries and softmax
md: Do not apply softmax before passing scores to `CrossEntropyLoss`. It would softmax them a second time, squashing the probabilities toward each other and weakening the gradients. Pass the raw logits.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Measuring a model: metrics, thresholds and cross-validation
md: Accuracy on imbalanced data is close to meaningless: always compare it with the "always the majority class" baseline. Report precision and recall (or a PR curve) for the rare class.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: What hidden units compute: hinges, cuts and new features
md: Misconception: universal approximation means one wide layer is all you need. It says suitable weights exist, not how many units that takes or that gradient descent will find them. The notes of CS231n, Stanford's course on convolutional neural networks for visual recognition, call it mathematically cute but a relatively weak statement in practice.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Training a real network: an MLP on handwritten digits
md: Nothing new happened here. The forward pass, softmax cross-entropy, BP1 to BP4 in batched form and the SGD step are the same ones you ran by hand on a 2-2-1 network; MNIST just has 79,510 parameters and 64 examples per batch.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Concurrency: race conditions and locks
md: Any read-modify-write (read a value, change it, write it back) of shared data (even `x++`) is several instructions, and a context switch can split them. Protect every critical section with a lock, and build locks on atomic hardware instructions, never on plain loads and stores.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Files and directories: the API and how vsfs finds your data
md: lseek() never moves the disk head. It only changes the offset stored in the open file table. A disk seek happens later, if the next read or write lands on a different track.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Bayes' rule: why a 90 percent accurate test is often wrong
md: Posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior. Strong evidence can be overwhelmed by a small prior, and the denominator just rescales so the posteriors sum to 1.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence
md: Check the log base before comparing numbers. Machine learning code and the Deep Learning book use the natural log (nats); information theory texts often use bits. Divide nats by $\ln 2 = 0.693$ to get bits.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Why loss falls on a straight line in log-log space
md: A scaling law turns each multiplicative step in scale into a fixed **ratio** of loss. Fit the exponent on cheap runs, then extrapolate. Small exponents (around 0.05 to 0.1 here) mean big scale-ups buy modest gains.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Inference cost, overtraining and where scaling laws break
md: Chinchilla-optimal answers one question: lowest loss per training FLOP. Real decisions also weigh inference volume, available data and downstream metrics, so production models are often smaller and trained on far more than 20 tokens per parameter.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Comparing systems honestly: judgment holes, variance, online tests
md: A test collection is a measuring instrument with known biases. Report the metric, cutoff and gain you used, look at per-query results, test significance with paired tests, and be suspicious when a genuinely new kind of system loses on an old pool.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Why language models read subwords, not words or characters
md: A subword tokenizer gives you short sequences for common text **and** no unknown words, because anything rare can always fall back to smaller pieces. Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) is the most widely used way to choose those pieces.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Special tokens, chat templates and prompt boundaries
md: Hugging Face tokenizers match special-token strings in any text by default, the opposite of tiktoken. If user text is tokenized with them, escape it or load the tokenizer with `split_special_tokens=True`. Also, a rendered template already contains its special tokens: the Transformers docs say to tokenize it with `add_special_tokens=False` so they are not added twice.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Learning rate: the stability limit, warmup, decay and clipping
md: Clipping must go **after** `loss.backward()`, which computes the gradients, and **before** `optimizer.step()`, which applies the update. Andrej Karpathy (whose training recipe is lesson 8) keeps a list of silent bugs that includes clipping the *loss* instead of the gradients, which simply ignores outlier examples instead of taming their updates.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Greedy search on a proximity graph, and why ef matters
md: $ef$ is the size of the result list W. A larger $ef$ explores more of the graph, escapes more local minima and raises recall, at the cost of more distance computations. To return $k$ results you need $ef \ge k$; hnswlib (the reference C++ and Python implementation of HNSW) documents that ef cannot be set lower than k.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Maintainer takeover: when the real publisher ships malware
md: For maintainers: phishing-resistant MFA (security keys or passkeys using WebAuthn, the W3C Web Authentication standard, which ties each login to the real site's domain so a lookalike page gets nothing usable), publish only from CI with trusted publishing, and disallow token publishes. For consumers: lockfiles, a release-age cooldown, and alerts on publisher changes.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Why resampling your own outputs erases rare events
md: Model collapse is not caused by a bad model or a bug. In this example fitting is exact. The finite sample alone, which Shumailov et al. call **statistical approximation error**, is enough to drive the process.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Synthetic data at scale: rephrasing, textbooks, reward-filtered SFT
md: At scale the recipe is the same as at small scale. Knowledge or judgment must come from outside the generator: real documents to rephrase (WRAP), real seeds and engineered variety (Cosmopedia), or a filter trained on human preferences and ground truth (Nemotron). Decontaminate against your evaluations.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: mmap: putting a file into your address space
md: mmap is lazy. The call sets up a promise; each page is paid for with a page fault on first touch. Errors that `read` would return as a value (file truncated, disk error) arrive as signals instead.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: When mmap wins, when it hurts, and how to steer it
md: Use mmap for read-mostly data that fits in memory and benefits from sharing. When data far exceeds memory, or you need control over when writes reach disk and how I/O errors surface, explicit I/O with your own buffer pool wins.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Merging overlapping roles: union, gaps and double counting
md: Total experience is the length of the union of role intervals, not the sum of their lengths. Sort by start, sweep, extend with max of the ends, and record gaps as you close blocks.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Verifiers set the ceiling: error rates, GenRM and self-verification
md: The false positive rate sets the ceiling, and it is multiplied by the number of wrong samples. At $p = 0.01$, even $t = 0.9$ and $f = 0.01$ give a ceiling of $0.009 / (0.009 + 0.0099) = 0.48$. Rare correct answers drown among rare false accepts: that is lesson 3's plateau, now as a formula.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Exchanging test-time compute for a bigger model
md: Test-time compute is a second scaling axis, not a replacement for the first. It pays most when the model can already sometimes solve the task and something can recognize a correct answer.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Large-chunk TTT, one map of the design space, and the costs
md: Common failure modes: (1) Wall-clock, not FLOPs, is the bottleneck. The TTT paper reports that TTT-MLP still faces challenges in memory I/O, and Titans' throughput falls roughly linearly with memory depth. (2) Inner learning rates that are too large make the memory diverge (lesson 2). (3) Without forgetting, a fixed-size memory overflows on long inputs. (4) Most published comparisons use models under 1.5B parameters.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: What threat hunting is, and the hunt that started at 75 cents
md: A hunt assumes the attacker is already inside and that existing alerts missed them, then tests that assumption against data. Its value is not only intrusions found: like Stoll's alarms on stolen account names, what a hunt learns should become a detection, a fix, or a request for better data.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: What threat intelligence is, and what it is for
md: A feed is not intelligence. 40,000 addresses with no dates, sources, context or relevance to you are data, and a lot of it is stale or shared infrastructure (recall the shared-IP and reputation-lag traps from the alert triage course). Buying more data does not produce more intelligence; analysis against a question does.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: STIX 2.1: threat intelligence as a graph
md: STIX makes sharing easy, including sharing mistakes. A wrong `attributed-to` edge, or an indicator without `valid_until` and confidence, propagates to every consumer automatically. Model uncertainty explicitly: use confidence, Opinion objects, and leave edges out when evidence is missing.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: STRIDE: six ways things go wrong
md: Each STRIDE letter names a broken property, and the property tells you the family of fix: spoofing needs authentication, tampering needs integrity checks, repudiation needs trustworthy logs, disclosure needs confidentiality controls, denial of service needs capacity and limits, elevation needs authorization.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Defence in depth and zero trust
md: Zero trust is not a product and does not mean trusting nothing. It means no trust from network location alone. You still trust identity providers, device management and the policy engine, so those become the crown jewels and need the strongest protection.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Naive, seasonal naive and simple exponential smoothing
md: A parameter fitted to minimize one-step in-sample error is not automatically good at the horizon you care about. Always evaluate at the real horizon on data the fit never saw.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Chains and roots: how a browser validates a certificate
md: Trust flows down from the trust store, never up from the server. Everything the server sends is just a candidate until a signature path connects it to a root you already had.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Fused softmax: one row per program, reductions on chip
md: This design assumes a whole row fits in one block; the tutorial targets matrices whose rows fit in on-chip memory. For very long rows you would loop over chunks of the row inside the program and combine partial maxima and sums instead.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: One encoder or two: why Janus splits seeing from drawing
md: Shared vs separate encoders is a trade between simplicity and specialization. One encoder means one token type and one path, but semantic and reconstruction goals pull against each other. Two encoders let each path pick its best tool while the transformer still sees one sequence.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Concurrency in one address space: cooperative threads and no fork
md: Cooperative scheduling has no time slices. Any loop that neither waits nor yields holds the only vCPU until it ends, starving every other request and timer in the unikernel.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Why one vector distance is mostly a memory problem
md: A common mistake is to benchmark a distance kernel on a few thousand vectors that fit in L2 cache and extrapolate to a 100 GB index. The small benchmark measures compute; the real index measures memory.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Why verl splits the RL loop from the GPU programs
md: The controller decides **what runs and in what order**; each WorkerGroup decides **how** it runs on its GPUs. That is why a new algorithm is a change to one Python loop, and a new backend or placement is a change to the workers or the config, never both.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Which frames to look at: uniform sampling and the needle problem
md: A hit is necessary, not sufficient. A sampled frame inside the event only gives the model a chance; it still has to recognize the content at the token resolution it was given. The formula is an upper bound on what sampling allows.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Where ViT-B/16's 86 million parameters live
md: Library checkpoints may differ slightly from this count. Hugging Face's `ViTModel` can include an extra pooler layer (a D x D dense plus tanh); `ViTForImageClassification` builds the backbone without it and reads the raw CLS state. Always check with a parameter count on the actual model rather than trusting a model card.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: Why per-step tokens break at 50 Hz, and how FAST compresses them
md: FAST spends tokens on information, not on time steps. Across datasets from 5 Hz to 50 Hz it produced roughly 30 tokens per arm per 1-second chunk, so the token count tracks the complexity of the motion rather than the control rate.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Token budgets: bits per image, 1D tokenizers and early fusion
md: TiTok's 32 tokens are not an image patch each. Flattening a 2D grid into a sequence still keeps the grid constraint; a 1D tokenizer lets each token describe any part of the image. Ids from different tokenizers are not interchangeable even at the same length.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Turning an image into tokens a language model can read
md: A VLM in the LLaVA style is just a language model whose input sequence contains extra tokens that came from an image. Every visual token costs context length and compute exactly like a text token.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Where VLMs fail and how they are evaluated
md: Treat a VLM as a strong but fallible reader: give it legible pixels, ask for fields it can copy rather than compute, and verify with rules the document itself provides.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Why learn the weather from 80 years of reanalysis
md: A common misconception is that these models learn from raw observations. They learn to imitate ERA5, so they inherit its biases (GraphCast excludes precipitation from its headline evaluation because ERA5 precipitation has known biases), and they start each forecast from an NWP analysis.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: The intercepting proxy: Burp Suite and ZAP as a workflow
md: A trusted proxy CA in your everyday browser is a standing risk, and a proxy pointed at the wrong host is unauthorised testing. Use a dedicated testing browser, set the target scope before you browse, and turn interception off when you are done.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Blind SSRF, out-of-band checks and server-side browsers
md: OAST proof should stop at the interaction. A DNS lookup or HTTP request to your Collaborator domain proves the fetch; reaching internal services, metadata or credentials on a production target goes beyond proof, and most policies want you to stop and report at that point.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: The same-origin policy: what it blocks and what it lets through
md: The same-origin policy limits what a page can **read** from other origins. It does not stop a page from **sending** requests to them, and it does nothing at all to code that is already running inside your origin. State-changing endpoints need their own protection on the server.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: The map: what happens when you open one file on Windows
md: Windows security is identity attached to processes. A process acts with the token it was given, so "which account ran this, and with which token" is the first question in almost every Windows investigation.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Patch Tuesday and PrintNightmare: closing holes on a schedule
md: Attack surface reduction: every service running as SYSTEM is a door. If a machine does not need a service (printing on a domain controller, SMBv1 anywhere, RDP on the internet), turn it off. You cannot be exploited through code that is not running.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Bluetooth and BLE: pairing, KNOB and BlueBorne
md: Bluetooth has two separate risk classes. Protocol design (pairing models, KNOB's unauthenticated negotiation) decides what a nearby listener or MITM can do to a correct implementation. Implementation bugs (BlueBorne) let a nearby attacker run code, with no pairing at all. Updates fix both; turning Bluetooth off removes the second.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Why a pool needs more than one shared queue
md: Work stealing moves the cost of load balancing onto idle workers. Busy workers pay almost nothing; the worker with nothing to do is the one that goes looking.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Cheap scaling studies, continual training and failure modes
md: WSD separates *making progress* (long constant LR trunk) from *cashing it in* (short cooldown). That separation is what makes checkpoints reusable, runs extendable and scaling studies roughly linear in the number of model sizes instead of quadratic.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: When zero-copy pays: measurements, limits and choices
md: Zero-copy pays when messages are large, the CPU is the bottleneck and the program does not touch the bytes. Any step that reads every byte (software checksums, encryption, hashing, compression) brings the copy back almost for free and erases most of the win.
